profile.campus: Stream Houston/The Woodlands, TX site (IAHA) - sold, no longer Stream-operated
profile.address: 4001 Technology Forest Boulevard, The Woodlands, TX 77381
profile.reading: Stream Data Centers Houston sits at 4001 Technology Forest Boulevard in The Woodlands, Texas, internally coded IAHA by the operator. Per Stream own site, the facility provided 7.8-plus megawatts of 2N critical load across a 10,000 square foot data hall within a larger building, opened in 2013 to a Tier III design standard and LEED Silver certified. Stream current locations page, however, describes this site as sold and now operating as a private data center no longer under Stream management, so this record documents the facility Stream-era history rather than its current operator or status. No tenant was named for the site during its Stream-operated years. Stream Data Centers was founded in 1999 in Dallas, Texas, originally as a technical real estate affiliate of Stream Realty Partners, a larger commercial real estate firm, confirming that lineage directly from Stream own company history page. Ownership has changed more recently: Apollo-managed funds announced acquisition of a majority stake in Stream in August 2025 and completed the deal in November 2025, with Principal Asset Management taking a minority stake and Stream management retaining a minority position, and Stream now describes itself as a key operating platform within the Apollo ecosystem. The company markets its wholesale, powered-shell, and build-to-suit data center model, claiming more than 90 percent of its capacity leased to Fortune 100 customers and describing a pipeline exceeding four gigawatts with more than 27 delivered developments across markets including Dallas-Fort Worth, Phoenix, Chicago, San Antonio, Atlanta, and historically Austin, Santa Clara, Denver, Minneapolis, and the Washington DC area. The Woodlands, a large master-planned community north of Houston, has grown into a significant secondary data center and corporate back-office market over the past two decades, driven partly by major energy-sector employers headquartered there, a pattern consistent with Stream original 2013-era decision to build in that submarket rather than closer to downtown Houston.
profile.research_note: 7.8+ MW 2N, 10,000 sqft data hall, 2013 opening, Tier III/LEED Silver sourced to Stream own Houston location page, which also states the site is now sold and no longer Stream-operated, noted explicitly. Company founding, Apollo/Principal Nov 2025 acquisition, and footprint sourced to Stream own history and news pages.
sources_tried: Streams own dedicated Houston/The Woodlands page, Streams own Apollo acquisition press release, and Apollos own completion press release

reading.body:
Stream Data Centers Houston has no published power capacity, making it impossible to assess its contribution to AI compute infrastructure or grid constraints despite its operator's national scale and recent acquisition by Apollo.

Stream Data Centers operates more than 20 campuses nationally with a 4 plus gigawatt development pipeline and reports over 90 percent of capacity leased to Fortune 100 customers. Apollo Global Management completed its majority acquisition on November 3, 2025, with Principal Asset Management and Stream's management retaining minority stakes. This ownership structure and customer base signal serious capital backing and operational stability. The Houston facility sits at 4001 Technology Forest Blvd in The Woodlands and is internally coded IAHA.

Texas hosts 133 mapped data center locations with 468.41 MW of disclosed capacity across 18 facilities. Stream Data Centers Houston does not appear in any published power rankings for the state. This absence means either its capacity remains undisclosed or falls below the smallest published figure available. Without a power specification from the operator's own documentation, no calculation is possible for its rank, share of state capacity, or racks and accelerators deployed there.

For readers tracking grid constraints on AI scaling, undisclosed capacity is functionally invisible. The facility's relevance depends entirely on whether Stream Data Centers publishes its power specification or whether independent measurement becomes available. Until then, the Houston campus cannot be counted in any assessment of available compute capacity in Texas or regionally.
